Shares of SoFi Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:SOFI) are trading flat Wednesday afternoon as investors weigh recent insider selling pressure against a major institutional milestone in the digital asset space.

Here’s what investors need to know.

  • SoFi Technologies stock is showing downward bias. Where are SOFI shares going?

Historic Mastercard Stablecoin Integration

On Sept. 22, SoFi expanded its digital payment capabilities by becoming the first OCC-regulated national bank to go live with stablecoin settlement across Mastercard’s global payments network. The integration effectively shifts an annualized $25 billion card program onto stablecoin rails, utilizing the bank’s proprietary SoFiUSD token.

Because SoFiUSD is issued directly by SoFi Bank and backed one-to-one by cash reserves, the backend migration allows the company to streamline cross-border settlement, free up trapped liquidity, and cut transaction latency. Crucially, the technology operates entirely beneath the swipe, meaning retail consumers and merchants do not need to hold digital assets, build new blockchain infrastructure, or alter their everyday payment habits.

"In six months, SoFi and Mastercard took stablecoin settlement from an idea to a live product that materially improves how money moves for businesses," said Anthony Noto, CEO of SoFi. "Merchants do not need to hold stablecoins, build new infrastructure or change how they operate. Through SoFi’s Big Business Banking platform, any merchant can receive settlement funds instantly in a SoFi Bank account and withdraw to cash around the clock and at zero cost. That means businesses have faster access to their money via the speed of blockchain, with the safeguards of a bank."

Moving forward, the companies plan to pursue additional SoFiUSD applications across the Mastercard ecosystem, specifically targeting cross-border payments and remittances. Furthermore, SoFi indicated it intends to offer these stablecoin settlement capabilities to external financial companies through its Galileo technology platform.

Payward Alliance Deepens Crypto Footprint

The Mastercard integration followed another corporate milestone earlier in the month. On Sept. 3, SoFi announced a strategic partnership with Payward Inc., the parent company of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken, to connect banking and digital asset markets.

Under the agreement, Payward joined the SoFi Exchange Network to list SoFiUSD on its multi-asset trading platform. Simultaneously, SoFi tapped Kraken Prime to serve as its primary engine for institutional digital asset trade execution. The dual-sided integration broadens SoFi’s liquidity pool and strengthens its footprint within the regulated digital asset ecosystem.

SOFI Stock Pauses Wednesday Afternoon

Editor’s note: This article was updated to reflect the downward revision in July’s annual core PCE inflation.

Inflation as measured by the Federal Reserve’s preferred came in cooler than expected last month, according to data released Wednesday by the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.3% month-over-month, below economists’ expectations of 0.4%.

On an annual basis, headline PCE inflation held at 3.4%, matching July’s revised reading and below the 3.7% consensus.

Core PCE, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.2% month-over-month, compared with a 0.3% forecast. The annual core rate came in at 3.0%, unchanged from July’s downwardly revised level, but below expectations of 3.3%.

At 3.0%, core inflation remains a full percentage point above the Fed’s 2% target.

The release included the BEA’s annual revisions, which also lowered past inflation. Core PCE prices rose at an annualized 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% previously estimated.

Second-quarter GDP growth was revised up, to 2.2% from 1.5%.

Traders see a 52.9% chance that the Fed will leave rates unchanged at 3.75%-4.00% on Oct. 28, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The probability of a quarter-point hike to 4.00%-4.25% stands at 47.1%.

Energy Drove the Monthly Gain in August

Energy was the biggest source of price pressure in August.

Prices for energy goods and services rose 2.3% on the month, after falling 1.4% in July. Gasoline and other energy goods led the increase, up 4.4%.

Goods prices overall rose 0.3%, reversing a 0.1% decline in July.

Food bought at grocery stores was flat.

Services prices rose 0.3%, up from 0.1% in July.

Transportation services rose 1.4%, the largest monthly gain in that category this year. Prices at restaurants and hotels rose 0.5%, after a 0.1% decline the previous month.

Some parts of the basket cooled.

Housing costs rose 0.2%, compared with 0.3% in July. Durable goods prices rose 0.1%, down from 0.4%.

Markets Welcome the Softer Print

Stocks and bonds rallied after the release.

As of 8:46 a.m. ET, S&P 500 futures were up 0.3% at 7,708.

Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.5%, while Dow futures gained 0.3%.

The small-cap Russell 2000 outperformed, rising 0.6%.

Treasury yields fell. The two-year yield, the most sensitive to Fed policy expectations, dropped about 4 basis points to 4.84%.

The U.S. Dollar Index slipped 0.2% to 100.70. Gold – tracked by the SPDR Gold Shares (NYSE:GLD) – rose 0.6% to $4,215 an ounce, and Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) gained 1.35% to about $84,927.

Shares of Fair Isaac Corp. (NYSE:FICO) extended losses in Wednesday afternoon trading, continuing a sharp sell-off triggered by federal regulatory changes and aggressive competitive pricing designed to break the company’s long-held monopoly over mortgage credit scoring.

Here’s what investors need to know.

  • Fair Isaac stock is showing notable weakness. What’s pressuring FICO stock?

FHFA Mandates Unified Mortgage Pricing Grid

The primary driver of the sell-off is a major policy shift announced late Monday by Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte. Pulte disclosed on X that government-sponsored enterprises Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are eliminating dual pricing structures in favor of a single unified pricing grid.

Under the revised mandate, the lower-cost VantageScore model will operate on the same pricing grid as the traditional FICO Classic model. The regulatory intervention directly follows repeated criticisms from Pulte regarding FICO’s elevated scoring fees, removing structural barriers for lenders seeking alternative credit scoring options.

TransUnion Price War Accelerates VantageScore Adoption

Compounding the regulatory overhang, credit bureau TransUnion (NYSE:TRU) extended its promotional 99-cent pricing for the VantageScore 4.0 model through December 2028. Under the extended structure, lenders can purchase standalone VantageScore 4.0 originations for 99 cents or receive the model at no additional charge when purchasing a standard FICO score.

The steep pricing discount has driven rapid market adoption across the mortgage sector. TransUnion reported that between January and September 2026, VantageScore integration expanded to more than 1,100 mortgage lenders, including nine of the 15 largest mortgage originators in the United States.

India’s market is being pulled in two directions.

The economy is producing numbers that suggest continued momentum. Financial markets are reacting to a very different set of signals: crude oil above $100 a barrel, a rupee near ₹96 to the dollar, rising inflation and heavy foreign selling.

That disconnect is becoming the central investment story for the final months of 2026.

India recorded 7.8% real GDP growth in the April-June quarter of FY27, beating the Reserve Bank of India’s earlier 7% estimate. Real gross value added grew 8.2%, while household consumption increased 7.1% and investment climbed 11.9%.

But the external environment is getting tougher.

Brent crude recently moved above $108 a barrel, while the rupee traded close to ₹96 per dollar. At the same time, foreign investors pulled $2.7 billion from Indian equities in September, taking total 2026 outflows to approximately $26.8 billion.

The question for investors is no longer whether India is growing.

It is whether that growth can absorb a much more expensive energy bill.

The Economy Has More Momentum Than The Market

The latest GDP data provide an important starting point.

India’s economy expanded 7.8% in Q1 FY27, its strongest first-quarter growth rate during the four-year period from FY24 through FY27. Manufacturing grew 9.1%, while services remained a major contributor to overall activity.

Investment is particularly important.

Gross fixed capital formation increased 11.9%, suggesting that companies and the government are continuing to spend on productive capacity despite global uncertainty.

Exports also grew 12%, while industrial production increased 6.7% in July. Credit growth provides another indication of domestic activity, with lending to industry rising 20% and services credit increasing 22.9% in July.

That combination gives India a meaningful domestic buffer.

The economy is not relying entirely on foreign capital or exports. Consumption, infrastructure spending, business investment and bank lending are all contributing to activity.

That becomes particularly important when external conditions deteriorate.

Oil Is The Vulnerability Investors Cannot Ignore

India’s problem with crude is structural.

The country imports roughly 90% of its crude oil requirements, leaving the economy highly sensitive to international energy prices.

When Brent moves from $80 to $100, the impact does not remain confined to fuel companies.

Higher crude prices increase the cost of transportation, logistics, chemicals, aviation and manufacturing. They can also widen India’s import bill and increase demand for U.S. dollars.

That creates pressure on the rupee.

The latest move illustrates the relationship. Brent rose to around $108.20 a barrel in late September as geopolitical tensions intensified, while the rupee weakened toward ₹96 per dollar. The Reserve Bank of India intervened to limit the currency’s decline.

For an economy that imports most of its crude, a weak currency effectively makes the oil shock more expensive.

This is where the two problems reinforce each other.

Inflation Has Become The Second Problem

India’s inflation data are not yet signaling a runaway price spiral, but the direction deserves attention.

Headline CPI inflation increased to 4.82% in August 2026, compared with 4.45% in July. Food inflation was higher at 5.95%, with rural food inflation reaching 6.13%.

That matters because food and fuel have a disproportionate effect on household budgets.

If expensive crude pushes transportation and distribution costs higher while food prices remain elevated, disposable income can come under pressure.

For investors, the concern is not simply inflation itself.

It is what inflation could force the RBI to do.

The central bank has less room to ease monetary policy if oil-driven inflation becomes persistent. Higher interest rates, in turn, can increase borrowing costs for companies and consumers just as businesses are investing heavily in capacity.

Foreign Investors Are Taking A More Defensive Position

The stock market is already reflecting some of these concerns.

The Nifty 50 declined 6.1% in September, while the Sensex fell 5.8%, making September the market’s weakest month since March. All 16 major sectors tracked in the latest Reuters report declined during the month.

Foreign investors have been a major source of pressure.

They sold approximately $26.8 billion of Indian equities during 2026, including $2.7 billion in September alone.

Several factors are behind that selling, including higher U.S. yields, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about India’s relative valuation.

Domestic investors, however, have continued providing support.

That difference is important. India’s equity market is no longer dependent on foreign institutional capital to the same extent as it was in earlier cycles. Domestic mutual funds, insurers and retail investors have become a much larger source of equity demand.

This does not eliminate volatility.

It can, however, provide a cushion when global investors reduce exposure.

The Rupee Has One Important Line Of Defence

The currency story also needs some context.

The rupee has fallen 0.7% in September and 1.2% during the July-September quarter, according to Reuters, making it one of Asia’s weaker currencies. Its record low stands at ₹96.96 per dollar.

Yet the RBI still has substantial tools available.

Policy measures introduced since June generated approximately $143.5 billion of foreign-currency inflows between June 8 and September 18. Those inflows helped push India’s reported foreign-exchange reserves to a record $785.7 billion.

The RBI has also used spot intervention and currency swaps to manage liquidity and exchange-rate volatility.

That does not mean the rupee cannot weaken further.

It means policymakers have a substantial buffer to prevent disorderly moves.

Where The Next Leg Of Growth Could Come From

The current environment may favor businesses with strong domestic demand, pricing power, foreign-currency revenues or direct exposure to government investment.

Infrastructure and capital goods remain closely tied to India’s investment cycle. With fixed capital formation up 11.9%, companies such as Larsen & Toubro remain exposed to spending on transportation, power, industrial projects and other infrastructure.

Banking is another area to monitor. With industry credit growing 20% and services credit 22.9%, lenders remain connected to India’s investment and working-capital requirements. HDFC Bank offers exposure to the country’s large private banking sector, although funding costs and asset quality remain important variables.

Defense manufacturing has a separate structural catalyst. India’s FY27 defense allocation is approximately ₹7.85 lakh crore, with defense capital expenditure around ₹2.19 lakh crore. Hindustan Aeronautics therefore remains closely linked to the government’s push toward domestic aerospace and defense production.

IT exporters offer a different currency dynamic. Companies such as Infosys earn substantial revenue in dollars, so rupee depreciation can support reported earnings and margins. But the benefit could be offset if U.S. technology spending weakens or AI changes demand for traditional outsourcing services.

The Risks Could Arrive From Several Directions

The biggest risk is duration.

If oil falls back quickly, India’s current pressures could prove manageable. If crude remains above $100 for several months, the consequences become more complicated.

A prolonged oil shock could push inflation higher, widen the import bill and increase pressure on the rupee.

Persistent foreign selling could amplify equity-market volatility.

A weaker monsoon or another food-supply disruption could compound the inflation problem.

Higher interest rates could eventually slow credit growth and private investment.

And if global growth weakens, India’s exporters could face pressure even while domestic demand remains relatively resilient.

These risks do not necessarily invalidate India’s longer-term growth story. They do change the path that growth may take.

Conclusion

India enters the final part of 2026 with a powerful combination of domestic growth and external pressure.

GDP is expanding at 7.8%, investment is growing 11.9%, industrial credit is rising 20%, and foreign-exchange reserves have reached a reported $785.7 billion.

At the same time, Brent crude has moved above $100, inflation has risen to 4.82%, the rupee is hovering near ₹96, and foreign investors have withdrawn approximately $26.8 billion from Indian equities this year.

That makes the next phase less about India’s ability to grow and more about the cost of maintaining that growth.

For investors, the distinction is important. A strong domestic economy can withstand an external shock, but companies will not all experience that shock in the same way.

Businesses with strong domestic demand, healthy balance sheets, pricing power, infrastructure exposure or dollar revenues may respond differently from companies heavily dependent on imported energy or discretionary consumption.

For U.S.-based NRIs, there is one additional consideration: a strong Indian equity return in rupees does not automatically translate into the same return in dollars.

The oil price, the rupee and India’s domestic growth rate are now interconnected parts of the same investment equation.

A cooler-than-expected reading on the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge has strengthened the case for Treasury bonds, after August data came in below economists’ forecasts, helped largely by downward revisions to prior months.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.3% month over month in August, below the 0.4% consensus estimate. Core PCE rose 0.2%, versus expectations of 0.3%.

On an annual basis, core PCE held at 3.0% in August, unchanged from July’s downwardly revised rate and below the 3.3% forecast, which was based on July’s pre-revision figure. The data pushed the two-year Treasury yield down about 4 basis points to 4.84%, as traders reassessed the path of Fed policy.

Why TLT Has More to Gain From Falling Yields

Lower yields put the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT) directly in focus.

Unlike an equity ETF, TLT’s sensitivity to interest rates comes from the bonds it owns. The fund invests primarily in U.S. Treasury bonds with remaining maturities of more than 20 years. Because those bonds have long maturities, their prices can move significantly when market yields change.

TLT currently has an effective duration of roughly 15 years. Duration provides a useful approximation of how much a bond portfolio’s price changes when yields move. In simple terms, a 1-percentage-point decline in yields would imply roughly a 15% increase in TLT’s underlying bond prices, before accounting for other factors. A 0.10-percentage-point decline would therefore imply roughly a 1.5% price increase, all else equal.

That makes TLT particularly relevant when inflation data changes expectations for the Fed and, consequently, Treasury yields.

The iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:IEF) offers a shorter-duration alternative. Because its Treasury holdings have less time remaining to maturity, its price is generally less sensitive to the same yield movement.

The Catch: Inflation Is Still Above Target

The PCE report isn’t an outright victory for the bond market. Core inflation at 3.0% remains a full percentage point above the Fed’s 2% target, while second-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%.

Energy prices also jumped 2.3% in August, with gasoline and other energy goods rising 4.4%.

That leaves TLT’s next move heavily dependent on whether cooler inflation readings lead to a sustained decline in long-term Treasury yields. If yields continue falling, TLT’s long duration gives it substantially more price sensitivity than intermediate-duration Treasury ETFs such as IEF.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said Wednesday it has launched a sweeping investigation into major artificial intelligence developers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, to examine whether their products could put consumers at risk. The move marks the agency’s first U.S. enforcement effort focused on so-called AI agents and follows a string of incidents that drew public attention in July.

The commission intends to send compulsory information requests and seek testimony from leaders at prominent AI labs, naming Anthropic, OpenAI and research group METR. The New York Post published the initial report.

Anthropic and OpenAI have turned to METR for outside reviews tied to security events involving agent-style systems, the official said. 

Separately, President Donald Trump met top AI executives Tuesday and the companies agreed to pursue voluntary standards. Trump has publicly dismissed some AI-related fears while pushing for U.S. leadership in the technology, Reuters noted.

Anthropic recently flagged "significant and unpredictable legal risks" tied to agentic AI in materials connected to its planned market debut.

According to Reuters, the FTC chair had already been uneasy about these firms before an episode in which OpenAI-built agents compromised the open-source site Hugging Face. The official said the matter escalated after the agents explored weaknesses in an AI coding platform and then carried out a broader intrusion.

FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said developers could face responsibility when they direct agents to run cybersecurity exercises that end in real-world breaches. He also argued at the Reuters Momentum AI event in Austin last week that regulators should lean on current statutes rather than rushing new AI-specific legislation.

The FTC can bring cases over unfair or deceptive conduct and has previously used that power in matters involving inadequate protections for consumer data.

Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) announced a multi-year deal worth more than $1 billion with Synopsys Inc. (NASDAQ:SNPS) Wednesday, expanding the chip-design technology behind AWS’s custom silicon push as it builds alternatives to processors from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA).

Amazon will become the lead customer for Synopsys’ new application-optimized silicon IP business, essentially reusable chip designs tailored to specific workloads.

The agreement also expands Amazon’s use of Synopsys software to design, simulate and test increasingly complex chips.

Synopsys and Amazon will tailor the software for Amazon’s Trainium AI chips and Graviton processors.

Why It Matters

Amazon has increasingly pitched custom chips as a way to improve the economics of AI computing.

“From Graviton to Trainium, purpose-built chips deliver better performance at lower cost because they’re designed for exactly what customers need,” Amazon custom-silicon chief Peter DeSantis said.

CEO Andy Jassy said earlier this year that virtually all AI had historically run on Nvidia chips but that “a new shift has started.”

Amazon estimates Trainium could eventually save it tens of billions of dollars in annual capital spending and give AWS several hundred basis points of operating-margin advantage compared with relying on other companies’ chips for AI inference. Jassy also said AWS intends to remain a major Nvidia partner.

Amazon’s custom-chip business has already surpassed a $25 billion annual revenue run rate and is growing at a triple-digit percentage year over year. Anthropic and OpenAI have made multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitments to Trainium.

What’s in It for Synopsys

The agreement moves Synopsys’ new business toward a license-plus-royalty model, giving it the potential to earn more as production volumes rise.

For scale, Synopsys’ Design IP business generated $1.75 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year, Reuters reported. Amazon’s new agreement is worth more than $1 billion, spread over multiple years.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction market traders still see Nvidia comfortably holding the top spot.

Nvidia has an 80% chance of ending 2026 as the world’s largest company by market capitalization on Polymarket, versus 15% for Apple and 6% for Alphabet, another major developer of custom AI chips. Amazon trades below 1%. The market has attracted about $7.6 million in volume.

ARK Invest earlier this year called Amazon a “sleeping giant” in custom silicon, highlighting the growing competition facing Nvidia.

Synopsys shares were up more than 3% Wednesday afternoon, while Amazon gained about 1.5%.

Bank of America says the race to build artificial-intelligence agents is the next big driver of chip demand. The bank now expects the market for AI data-center systems to reach $2.2 trillion by 2030, up from a prior forecast of $1.8 trillion.

That implies growth of about 40% a year from 2026, compared with 33% in the old model.

The question for investors is which chip stocks stand to capture the most of it as the year enters its final quarter.

Best Semiconductor Stocks to Own In the Q4

In a note shared to clients on Wednesday, Bank of America’s analyst Vivek Arya named five top semiconductor picks with near-term catalysts:

  • Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA),
  • Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC),
  • Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU),
  • Marvell Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL)
  • Lam Research Corp. (NASDAQ:LRCX).

The bank also likes Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT), Analog Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:ADI) and ON Semiconductor Corp. (NASDAQ:ON).

Timing is part of the call.

From 2010 to 2025, the fourth and first quarters were the two best seasons to own chip stocks.

In those quarters, chip stocks beat the S&P 500 by a median of 3 to 5 percentage points.

Valuation is the other part.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index, a basket of the largest U.S.-listed chipmakers, trades at 21 times forward earnings. In other words, investors pay $21 for every dollar of profit expected over the next 12 months.

The index’s median multiple since ChatGPT launched is 24 times. As a result, the index trades about 12% below that level, while the bank projects earnings growth of 40% or more.

Why AI Agents Could Need More Chips, Not Fewer

AI agents are programs that carry out multi-step tasks on their own, such as writing and testing code.

According to the bank, a single agent workflow can generate 10 to 1,000 times more tokens, the units of text an AI model processes, than a chat exchange.

More tokens means more computing.

Arya said agent adoption, competition between AI labs and tight chip supply “will likely keep AI spending robust for the next several years.”

Meanwhile, Bank of America expects the biggest U.S. and Chinese cloud providers, plus newer AI cloud firms, to spend about $1 trillion on capital projects in 2026, roughly double last year.

That figure rises to $1.4 trillion in 2027.

Michael Saylor says Bitcoin treasury rivals like Strive (NASDAQ:ASST) aren’t competition for Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) — they’re allies.

Why Saylor Says Competitors Can Help Each Other

Saylor wrote in a lengthy post on X Wednesday that Strategy and Strive both build their businesses on the same foundation: Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) as capital, credit products like STRC and SATA, and equity like MSTR and ASST. 

Even though the two compete for the same investor dollars, Saylor argues their real opportunity lies outside the industry entirely.

He pointed to SIFMA data showing global equity markets hit $157.8 trillion and global fixed-income debt reached $160.7 trillion by the end of 2025. 

Just one-tenth of one percent of either market equals roughly $160 billion, which Saylor says is the real scale Bitcoin treasury companies should be chasing instead of fighting each other for scraps.

How a Rising Bitcoin Price Helps Everyone

Saylor’s argument comes down to three ways Bitcoin companies lift each other up.

  • Bitcoin demand lifts everyone — when any company buys Bitcoin, it adds demand for a fixed-supply asset. If that pushes the price higher, every holder benefits, not just the buyer. Saylor cites Strive’s $50 million purchase of Strategy’s STRC preferred stock in March as proof these companies already act as each other’s customers.
  • Credit products build trust together — as more products like STRC and SATA build a track record, investors get comfortable with the category, lowering borrowing costs across the board.
  • Proven models lift valuations — as more companies show the business actually works, equity investors gain confidence, lifting valuations for everyone doing it well.

Why More Competitors Actually Grow the Pie

Saylor compared the setup to the early auto industry, where Ford and oil companies like Standard Oil grew together rather than at each other’s expense. 

More cars created demand for fuel, and better fuel access made cars more useful. 

He argues Bitcoin treasury companies need the same kind of complementary ecosystem, with capital, credit, equity, and payments infrastructure all reinforcing one another.

He closed by tying the benefit directly to standards. A weak, poorly run issuer can hurt trust across the entire category, while a strong one builds it. 

Saylor said he welcomes any capable company willing to compete responsibly, calling it a model where good execution from any player strengthens the whole industry rather than just the individual firm.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is moving to clarify whether prediction market contracts are financial products or gambling, sending two new rules to the White House for review.

The agency submitted both rules Monday, according to White House regulatory filings.

One would treat event contracts as swaps, putting them under federal derivatives law. The other would exclude “casino-style gambling products” from the swap definition.

The event-contract rule would first go through public comment. The casino-gambling rule could take effect much sooner.

The move comes three days after a federal appeals court rejected Kalshi‘s argument that its sports contracts are swaps, a type of derivative that federal law places under the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction.

The fight matters for Robinhood Markets Inc. (NASDAQ:HOOD), which generated $156 million from event contracts in the second quarter, more than it made from equities or cryptocurrency trading.

Robinhood offers prediction-market contracts through federally regulated exchanges, putting the company in the middle of the same state-versus-federal fight now playing out around Kalshi.

Kalshi Just Lost This Argument

The Sixth Circuit ruled Friday that Kalshi’s sports-event contracts do not qualify as swaps because the sporting events underneath them are not inherently financial or economic.

The court said interest rate changes naturally carry financial consequences. Sports results may affect broadcasters, sponsors or local businesses, but those downstream effects are not enough to make a contract on the event a swap.

The ruling affirmed Ohio’s victory and lifted an injunction preventing Tennessee from enforcing its gambling laws, handing Kalshi another major legal setback.

The court went further, holding that even if Kalshi’s contracts were swaps, federal commodities law would not preempt Ohio’s or Tennessee’s gambling laws, meaning a new swap definition alone may not settle the fight in those states.

Federal courts have split on the issue. The Third Circuit sided with Kalshi in New Jersey in April, while the Ninth and Sixth circuits have ruled against it.

Where Do Sports Fit?

CFTC Chairman Michael Selig has repeatedly argued that prediction markets, including the sports contracts at the center of Kalshi’s state battles, fall under the agency’s exclusive jurisdiction.

The unanswered question is how the new rules will put that position into law. The full text has not been published, leaving unclear how the CFTC will distinguish sports event contracts from the “casino-style gambling products” it wants excluded from the swap definition.
